description: Containers for a Java developer: what an image and a container really are, writing a lean and safe Dockerfile for a Spring Boot service, networking, volumes, memory limits and the JVM, and debugging a container that dies or will not start.

cards.front: What is the difference between an image and a container?
cards.back: An image is a read-only template made of layers. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own thin writable layer on top.
cards.explanation: You can start many containers from one image. Anything written inside the container's filesystem lives in its writable layer and is lost when the container is removed. That is why databases and uploads need volumes. Rebuilding an image never changes containers that are already running; you must recreate them.
cards.example: docker run -d --name api-1 myorg/orders:1.4.2 and docker run -d --name api-2 myorg/orders:1.4.2 share the same image layers on disk.

cards.front: Is a container a lightweight virtual machine?
cards.back: No. A container is an ordinary Linux process isolated with namespaces (what it can see) and limited with cgroups (what it can use). It shares the host kernel.
cards.explanation: A VM boots its own kernel on virtual hardware. A container starts as fast as a process because it is one. Sharing the kernel is why a container built for linux/amd64 cannot natively run on an arm64 host without emulation, and why a kernel exploit is a bigger risk than a VM escape. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs a small Linux VM and your containers run inside it.
cards.example: ps aux on the Linux host shows the java process from inside your container, with a different PID than the container sees.

cards.front: How does the build cache decide which Dockerfile steps to rerun?
cards.back: Each instruction becomes a layer. If an instruction and everything before it are unchanged, Docker reuses the cached layer. The first changed instruction and every instruction after it rebuild.
cards.explanation: Order your Dockerfile from least to most frequently changed. Copy the build file (pom.xml or build.gradle) and download dependencies before you copy the source. Then a code change reuses the dependency layer instead of downloading the internet again. COPY . . near the top invalidates the cache on every commit.
cards.example:
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -q package -DskipTests

cards.front: Why use a multi-stage build for a Java service?
cards.back: The first stage has the JDK and Maven or Gradle and builds the jar. The final stage starts from a small JRE image and copies only the jar. Build tools and source never ship to production.
cards.explanation: A JDK plus Maven plus the ~/.m2 cache can be over a gigabyte. The runtime only needs a JRE and the artifact. Smaller images pull faster during a deploy and have fewer packages to patch for vulnerabilities. Name stages with AS so COPY --from=build is readable.
cards.example:
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build
...
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
COPY --from=build /app/target/orders.jar /app/orders.jar

cards.front: What does .dockerignore protect you from?
cards.back: It excludes files from the build context sent to the Docker daemon. Without it, target/, .git, IDE folders, and local secrets like .env are uploaded and can end up in the image.
cards.explanation: A large build context slows every build before the first instruction even runs. Worse, COPY . . will happily bake a .env file or credentials into a layer, and deleting it in a later RUN does not remove it from the earlier layer. Anyone who pulls the image can extract it.

cards.front: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
cards.back: ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs. CMD supplies default arguments, or a default command if there is no ENTRYPOINT. Arguments after the image name in docker run replace CMD, not ENTRYPOINT.
cards.explanation: A common pattern is ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/orders.jar"] with no CMD, or CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=prod"] as overridable defaults. Override the entrypoint itself only with docker run --entrypoint, which is useful for debugging (--entrypoint sh).
cards.example: docker run myorg/orders --server.port=9090 appends that argument to the ENTRYPOINT.

cards.front: Why should ENTRYPOINT use the exec form (JSON array) instead of the shell form?
cards.back: The exec form makes java PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM directly when the container stops. The shell form wraps it in /bin/sh -c, and the shell usually does not forward the signal.
cards.explanation: docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits (10 seconds by default), then sends SIGKILL. If java never sees SIGTERM, Spring Boot cannot finish in-flight requests or close connections, and every deploy kills requests mid-flight. If you need a shell script, end it with exec java ... so java replaces the shell. Spring Boot's graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful) only helps if the signal arrives.
cards.example:
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/orders.jar"]  (exec form)
ENTRYPOINT java -jar /app/orders.jar  (shell form: avoid)

cards.front: Why should a container not run as root?
cards.back: If an attacker gets code execution in your app, root inside the container makes escaping to the host or reading mounted secrets much easier. Create a user and switch to it with USER.
cards.explanation: Root in the container is the same UID 0 as root on the host unless user namespaces are configured. Many platforms (Kubernetes with restricted policies, OpenShift) refuse root containers outright. Make sure the app's files are readable by that user and that it does not need to bind ports below 1024. Spring Boot on 8080 is fine.

cards.front: Why is the latest tag dangerous in deployment files?
cards.back: latest is just a default tag name, not 'the newest build'. It moves when someone pushes it. Two servers can run different code under the same tag, and a rollback has nothing stable to return to.
cards.explanation: Tag images with something immutable: the git commit SHA or a version like 1.4.2. For maximum certainty, deploy by digest (image@sha256:...), which identifies exact bytes. Using latest on base images (FROM eclipse-temurin:latest) also means your build changes Java versions without a code change.

cards.front: How does the JVM decide its heap size inside a container?
cards.back: Modern JVMs are container-aware: they read the cgroup memory limit. By default the max heap is 25% of that limit (MaxRAMPercentage=25).
cards.explanation: Container support is on by default since JDK 10 and was backported to 8u191. 25% is conservative for a container that only runs one Java process. Many teams set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so the heap uses most of the limit while leaving room for metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers, and the GC's own memory. Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit is a classic mistake: the heap is not the only memory the JVM uses.
cards.example: docker run -m 1g myorg/orders with JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75" gives roughly a 768 MB heap.

cards.front: A container keeps restarting and docker inspect shows exit code 137 and OOMKilled: true. What happened?
cards.back: The kernel killed the process because the container exceeded its memory limit. 137 is 128 + 9, meaning SIGKILL. The JVM did not get to throw OutOfMemoryError or write a heap dump.
cards.explanation: This is different from java.lang.OutOfMemoryError, which happens inside the JVM when the heap is full. An OOMKill means total process memory (heap plus everything else) crossed the cgroup limit. Fixes: lower the heap percentage so off-heap memory fits, raise the limit, or find the off-heap growth (threads, direct buffers, native libraries) with Native Memory Tracking. Exit code 143 (128 + 15) means a normal SIGTERM.

cards.front: Why can a Java service in a container see far more CPUs than it is allowed to use, and why does that matter?
cards.back: A CPU limit (--cpus) throttles CPU time. Modern JVMs read it and size things like GC threads and the common ForkJoinPool from it, but an old JVM or an app that hard-codes thread counts from the host's core count will oversubscribe.
cards.explanation: If a JVM thinks it has 64 cores while limited to 2, it creates too many GC and pool threads, and the container gets throttled, showing up as random latency spikes. Check Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() inside the container. -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N overrides the detection when needed.

cards.front: What is the difference between a bind mount and a named volume?
cards.back: A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container. A named volume is storage managed by Docker, referenced by name, and independent of the host's directory layout.
cards.explanation: Use named volumes for database data in local development and anything you want to survive container removal. Use bind mounts to mount source code or config you are editing. Bind mounts depend on host paths and file permissions, which differ between laptops and CI. docker compose down -v deletes named volumes, which deletes your local database.
cards.example:
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16   (named volume)
docker run -v $(pwd)/config:/app/config myorg/orders   (bind mount)

cards.front: Inside a container, why does connecting to localhost:5432 fail to reach Postgres running in another container?
cards.back: localhost inside a container is that container itself. Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by service or container name, such as postgres:5432.
cards.explanation: Docker Compose creates a network for the project and registers each service name in its DNS. So spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/orders works between services. To reach something on your laptop from a container, Docker Desktop provides host.docker.internal. Publishing a port (-p 5432:5432) is for the host to reach the container, not for container-to-container traffic.

cards.front: What does -p 8080:8080 actually do, and what does EXPOSE do?
cards.back: -p host:container publishes a container port on the host. EXPOSE in a Dockerfile only documents which port the app listens on. It publishes nothing.
cards.explanation: The app must listen on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1, inside the container, or the published port connects to nothing. Spring Boot listens on all interfaces by default. -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 publishes only to the host's loopback, which is safer on a shared machine.

cards.front: What does depends_on in Docker Compose guarantee?
cards.back: By default only start order: the dependency's container has started. It does not wait until Postgres is ready to accept connections.
cards.explanation: Add a healthcheck to the dependency and use depends_on with condition: service_healthy. Even then, your application should retry its database connection at startup. In production on Kubernetes there is no depends_on at all, so retrying is the real fix and Compose ordering is a local convenience.

cards.front: A container exits immediately after docker run. How do you find out why?
cards.back: docker ps -a to see the exit code, docker logs <container> for its output, and docker inspect for the state, the command that ran, and OOMKilled.
cards.explanation: Common causes: the main process finished (a container lives only as long as PID 1), a missing environment variable crashed Spring at startup, the jar path in ENTRYPOINT is wrong, or the image was built for another CPU architecture (exec format error). To look around, override the entrypoint: docker run -it --entrypoint sh myorg/orders.
cards.example:
docker ps -a --filter name=orders
docker logs --tail 100 orders

cards.front: How do you open a shell inside a running container, and what if the image has no shell?
cards.back: docker exec -it <container> sh (or bash if installed). Distroless and minimal images have no shell, so attach a debug container that shares its namespaces, or debug from outside.
cards.explanation: exec starts a new process next to your app; it does not restart anything. With no shell, you can still use docker cp to copy files out, docker logs, and on Kubernetes kubectl debug with an ephemeral container. For Java, jcmd from a JDK-based debug image sharing the process namespace can still take thread and heap dumps.
cards.example:
docker exec -it orders sh
docker cp orders:/tmp/heap.hprof ./heap.hprof

cards.front: What does a HEALTHCHECK do, and what should a Java service's health check actually test?
cards.back: HEALTHCHECK runs a command periodically and marks the container healthy or unhealthy. For a Spring Boot service, call an endpoint like /actuator/health that reflects whether the app can serve requests.
cards.explanation: A check that only opens the TCP port passes while the app is deadlocked or cannot reach its database. Do not make liveness checks depend on downstream services, though, or one slow database restarts every container at once. Kubernetes separates liveness (restart me) from readiness (stop sending me traffic) for exactly this reason. Spring Boot exposes both as /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness.

cards.front: Where should secrets come from in a container, and where should they never be?
cards.back: Inject them at runtime: environment variables from the orchestrator's secret store, or mounted secret files. Never put them in the Dockerfile, an ENV line, a build ARG, or a copied file.
cards.explanation: Everything in a Dockerfile ends up in image metadata or layers, and docker history or docker inspect reveals ENV and ARG values. Anyone who can pull the image can read them. Build-time secrets (for a private Maven repo) should use BuildKit's --secret mount, which is not stored in a layer. Rotate any secret that was ever baked into a pushed image.

cards.front: Why does the container log driver want your Java service to log to stdout?
cards.back: Docker captures stdout and stderr of PID 1. Platforms ship those streams to the logging system. Logs written to a file inside the container are invisible to docker logs and disappear with the container.
cards.explanation: Twelve-factor style: the app writes events to stdout, the platform routes them. Writing to a file also grows the writable layer until the disk fills. Structured JSON logs make searching easier. Configure Logback with a console appender and avoid rolling file appenders in containers.

cards.front: What is the difference between docker stop and docker kill?
cards.back: docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits for the grace period (10 seconds by default), then sends SIGKILL. docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately unless you choose a signal.
cards.explanation: SIGKILL cannot be caught: no shutdown hooks, no flushing, no finishing requests. Always prefer stop. If your service needs longer to drain, raise the grace period with docker stop -t 30 or stop_grace_period in Compose, and keep it longer than Spring's spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase.

cards.front: What does a restart policy do, and why can it hide a bug?
cards.back: --restart unless-stopped (or on-failure, always) restarts a container when it exits. It keeps a crashing service 'up', which can mask a startup crash loop.
cards.explanation: Check docker ps for a RestartCount that keeps climbing or a status like 'Restarting (1) 5 seconds ago'. A crash loop that restarts every few seconds looks healthy in a dashboard that only checks 'is it running'. Alert on restart counts. Kubernetes reports this as CrashLoopBackOff.

cards.front: Your laptop is an Apple Silicon Mac and the server is x86. What can go wrong with images you build locally?
cards.back: docker build on an M-series Mac produces linux/arm64 images by default. Pushing that and running it on an amd64 server fails with 'exec format error' or runs slowly under emulation.
cards.explanation: Build for the target explicitly with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64, or build multi-architecture images for both. Let CI build release images rather than laptops. Base images like eclipse-temurin publish both architectures, so the source of the mismatch is usually your build command.

cards.front: How do you see what is using space and clean up safely?
cards.back: docker system df shows space used by images, containers, volumes, and build cache. docker image prune removes dangling images; docker builder prune clears build cache.
cards.explanation: docker system prune -a --volumes is the nuclear option. It deletes stopped containers, all unused images, and unused volumes, including your local database data. Read the confirmation prompt. On CI agents, scheduled pruning prevents 'no space left on device' build failures.
cards.example:
docker system df
docker image prune
docker builder prune --keep-storage 10GB

cards.front: Why choose a JRE base image like eclipse-temurin:17-jre over a full JDK image at runtime?
cards.back: The runtime only needs to run bytecode. A JRE image is smaller and has fewer tools an attacker could use. Use the JDK image only in the build stage.
cards.explanation: The trade-off: diagnostic tools like jcmd, jstack, and jmap come with the JDK. With a JRE image you trigger diagnostics through other means (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS for heap-dump-on-OOM, JFR settings, Actuator endpoints) or attach a JDK debug container. Some teams ship a JDK image for exactly this reason. Choose deliberately and document it.
cards.example:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre (runtime)
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jdk AS build (build stage)

cards.front: How do you pass JVM flags to a container without rebuilding the image?
cards.back: Set the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS environment variable. The JVM reads it at startup and prints 'Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS' to confirm.
cards.explanation: This keeps memory, GC, and diagnostic flags in deployment config instead of the Dockerfile. Useful set for production: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError. Mount /dumps as a volume or the dump disappears with the container.

cards.front: What is Testcontainers, and why do Java teams prefer it over an in-memory database in tests?
cards.back: A library that starts real dependencies (Postgres, Kafka, Redis) in Docker for an integration test and throws them away afterwards.
cards.explanation: H2 in Postgres compatibility mode is not Postgres: JSON operators, locking, and SQL dialect details differ, so tests pass and production fails. Testcontainers gives you the same engine and version as production. Cost: tests need a Docker daemon and start a little slower. Reuse one container per test class or suite to keep it fast.

cards.text: A container exit code of {{c1::137}} means the process received SIGKILL, often from the out-of-memory killer.
cards.extra: 128 + 9. Check docker inspect for OOMKilled: true. Exit code 143 (128 + 15) is a normal SIGTERM shutdown.

cards.text: By default, a container-aware JVM sets the max heap to {{c1::25%}} of the container memory limit.
cards.extra: Raise it with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, commonly 70 to 75 for a one-process container. Leave room for off-heap memory.

cards.text: Use the {{c1::exec}} form of ENTRYPOINT so java is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM.
cards.extra: Exec form is a JSON array: ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]. The shell form wraps java in sh, which usually swallows the signal.

cards.text: Copy {{c1::pom.xml}} and download dependencies before copying src so code changes reuse the cached dependency layer.
cards.extra: Docker rebuilds every layer after the first changed instruction. Order the Dockerfile from least to most frequently changed.

cards.text: Between Compose services, connect to {{c1::the service name}}, not localhost.
cards.extra: localhost inside a container is that container. Compose registers each service name in the project network's DNS.

cards.front: Write the outline of a production-ready Dockerfile for a Spring Boot jar.
cards.back: Multi-stage: a JDK build stage that caches dependencies then packages, and a JRE runtime stage that copies only the jar, runs as a non-root user, and starts java with an exec-form ENTRYPOINT.
cards.explanation: Add JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS for memory and heap dumps through deployment config rather than hard-coding. Pin base image versions. Keep a .dockerignore. Spring Boot can also split the jar into layers (dependencies, application) so that a code change only replaces the small application layer when pushing.
cards.example:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
COPY .mvn .mvn
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
